prompt.text:
Build a complete, polished browser horror game inspired by the "survive the night shift in a security office" genre (like Five Nights at Freddy's), but with a 100% ORIGINAL setting, characters, and name. Do not use any FNAF names, characters, locations, or assets.

## Concept
Title: "SUNNY HOLLOW: AFTER HOURS"
You are a night watchman at Sunny Hollow Studios, an abandoned 1990s children's TV studio. The show's animatronic puppet hosts were shut down after the show was cancelled (last live broadcast: May 17, 1996), but at night they still try to "finish the broadcast". Survive from 12 AM to 6 AM in a small control booth using cameras, shutters, door lights, a ceiling-vent seal and an audio lure, while managing a draining generator.

## Tech
- Single self-contained index.html (HTML + CSS + JS). Three.js r128 UMD from cdnjs (https://t.co/TUKtvoq6na). No external assets: all models are low-poly primitives, all textures are procedural canvas textures (felt, wood, rust, tiles, wallpaper, posters), all sound is generated with the Web Audio API.
- Desktop Chrome at 60 fps. Mouse controls plus keyboard shortcuts.
- Every room is its own THREE.Scene with its own camera, so only the viewed room is rendered. Pre-compile all shaders at boot (renderer.compile on every scene, with the puppets temporarily added) so the first camera flip doesn't hitch.
- Adaptive resolution: render the 3D into a render target at 0.85x. If the average frame time stays above 25 ms for 2.5 s, drop the internal scale by 0.15 (minimum 0.5).
- Add `[hidden]{display:none!important}` to the CSS so hidden overlay screens never block clicks.
- Save progress in localStorage (current night, beaten nights, stars, unlocks, custom-night sliders), wrapped in try/catch.

## Post-processing (full-screen shader)
VHS/CRT pass over everything: scanlines, film grain, chromatic aberration, a rolling tracking band, line jitter, vignette, a full-static mix, a red flash and a darkness fade. Use three presets: office (subtle), camera (strong scanlines, barrel distortion, green tint, more noise) and menu.

## Core loop
- 1 in-game hour = 60 real seconds (12 AM → 6 AM = 6 minutes).
- Mouse near the left/right 22% of the screen turns the view smoothly. Yaw is clamped to ±60°. Arrow keys work as a backup.
- Generator: 100% at start. Usage = 1 (base) + tablet 1 + each door light 1 + each closed shutter 2 + vent seal 1 + lure 1 (for 3 s). Drain = usage × 0.1% per second × night multiplier (N1 0.9, N2 0.95, N3 1.0, N4 1.03, N5 1.06, N6 1.14, custom 1.1). Show POWER LEFT % and colored usage bars.
- At 0%: shutters open, all lights die, cameras disabled. After 4–9 s Mr. Antler appears in the left doorway with eyes pulsing to a generated music-box melody (5–18 s), then 2 s of total darkness, then a jumpscare. If 6 AM arrives first, the player wins.
- 6 AM: chime, a "5 → 6 AM" rolling-digit screen, then the next night starts automatically.
- AI levels rise +1 at 2, 3 and 4 AM on nights 2+.

## Control booth (3D)
- Left and right doorways open onto dark corridors. Each doorway has a corrugated metal shutter that slides down, plus a wall panel with a red SHUTTER button and a white LIGHT button (hold).
- Without the light, a puppet in the doorway shows only faint glowing eyes. Office lights must have short range so the doorway stays dark.
- Desk: old CRT TV with rabbit ears (clickable), two static monitors, a spinning fan, a red phone (click to mute the call), a mug, papers, a desk lamp, a VENT SEAL lever box with an LED, and a tiny moose bobblehead.
- Front wall: a ceiling vent (real hole in the wall mesh, a duct behind it, angled slats, and a metal plate that slides down to seal it), a wall clock synced to game time, show posters, a "MAY 1996" calendar with the 17th circled, a kid's crayon drawing and a caution poster.
- A flickering fluorescent tube and hanging cables.

## Camera tablet
- Toggle with SPACE or by hovering the bottom bar.
- IMPORTANT, avoid a flicker bug: do NOT use mouseenter/mouseleave on the two bars (CAMERAS / LOWER sit in the same spot and ping-pong the tablet). Detect the bar zone from the pointer position inside a global pointermove handler. Flip once per visit (450 ms cooldown). Re-arm only after the mouse moves well above the bar (y < innerHeight − 110). Start each night disarmed.
- 0.22 s slide-up animation. The camera feed starts rendering once it's fully up.
- 8 cameras on a clickable schematic minimap (keys 1–8). Centered header shows "CAM 04 · WEST HALL" plus "● REC" and a timestamp. Slow camera pan in each room. A static burst on switch and whenever a puppet enters or leaves the viewed room.
- Tablet buttons: "♪ PLAY JINGLE [L]" (15 s cooldown bar) and "VENT: OPEN/SEALED [V]".
- Raising the tablet turns off held lights. Shutters can't be operated while it's up.

## Map
CAM 1 Main Stage (stage, painted sunny backdrop, teal curtains, talk-show desk, audience seats, APPLAUSE sign), CAM 2 Green Room, CAM 3 Prop Storage, CAM 4 West Hall, CAM 5 East Hall, CAM 6 Costume Closet, CAM 7 Vent Shaft (red emergency light), CAM 8 Broadcast Tower Room (equipment racks with LEDs, a wall of static/countdown CRTs, an ON AIR sign that lights up during the TV event).

## Antagonists (original, each with a unique mechanic)
Movement opportunity every ~5 s: move if random(0..20) < AI level.
1. MR. ANTLER: felt moose talk-show host (maroon blazer, yellow bow tie, palmate antlers, droopy eyelids, microphone). Route 1 → 2/3 → 4 → left door. He will NOT move while you watch his current camera. In the West Hall he walks toward the camera only while unwatched. At the door he waits lerp(10, 4.5, AI/20) s: shutter closed → loud bangs, he retreats to CAM 2/3. Open → jumpscare.
2. SPROCKET: tin robot co-host (rusty can head, bulb eyes, blinking antenna, chest dials, cassette slot). Route 1 → 8 → 5 → right door. Playing the jingle on a camera 1–2 steps behind him pulls him back there (15% chance the tape skips). Three successful lures within ~40 s each jam his tape for 25 s: red eyes, jittering, +5 aggression, lures stop working. At the right door he behaves like Antler (shutter blocks).
3. LULU: pink-striped sock marionette with button eyes, yarn hair and a wooden control bar with strings. Lives in CAM 6 with an unrest meter (+AI×0.14 per second unwatched, −9 per second while watched). Four visible poses (deeper in the closet → leaning out → staring at the camera); her pose only updates while unwatched. At 100 she enters the vent shaft, and her progress freezes while CAM 7 is watched. At the booth vent she scratches for 3.5–6 s: sealed → thump and she returns to the closet. Open → jumpscare.
4. THE UNDERSTUDY: faceless grey spare mascot suit, "SPARE #2" tag. Normally standing in CAM 3. When power is below 30% it can appear in a front corner of the booth (opposite the side you're facing), with flickering lights and breathing. Keep it out of view (turn away or raise the tablet) for 3 continuous seconds and it vanishes. Otherwise it gets you after lerp(12, 7, AI/20) s.
5. THE BROADCAST (night 5+): the booth TV turns on by itself with color bars and a countdown with beeps. Press T or click the TV before it ends. If it finishes, every camera shows "NO SIGNAL" for 10 s and Antler and Sprocket get +3 aggression meanwhile.

AI per night [Antler, Sprocket, Lulu, Understudy, Broadcast]:
N1 3,2,0,0,0 · N2 5,4,3,0,0 · N3 7,6,6,4,0 · N4 10,9,9,7,0 · N5 13,12,12,11,10 · N6 18,17,17,16,15.

## Jumpscares
The puppet lunges from 1.6 m to face distance in 0.22 s, head aligned to eye level, lit by a strong light. Camera shake, heavy chroma/jitter, a short red flash, and a loud synthesized screech (detuned sawtooths with LFO + distortion + noise). After ~1.35 s show "TECHNICAL DIFFICULTIES" over color bars and static, with who got you, a one-line tip, RETRY and MENU.

## Audio (all synthesized)
Generator hum, fan noise, camera hiss, light buzz, panned footsteps (Antler left, metallic clanks for Sprocket right), shutter slams, bangs, vent scratching, breathing, a cheerful-but-detuned show jingle (lowpassed and panned to the camera's side), the music box, a 6 AM chime with distant cheering, ambient creaks/drips/whispers/distant kids, and a menu drone. Start audio from the first click.

## Story
Each night a phone call types out 3–4 lines with a muffled formant "voice" synced word by word; it can be muted. The calls gradually reveal the lore: the nine-minute feed cut on May 17, 1996; the hosts found smiling at the camera; recordings of kids counting down; the previous watchman calling from inside the Tower Room on night 5. Night 6 is an automated station message.

## Menus and progression
- Boot screen "▶ PLAY TAPE".
- Main menu: a dark 3D stage with the hosts on the right side, a glitching yellow show logo, NEW GAME (with an erase confirmation), CONTINUE, NIGHT 6 and CUSTOM NIGHT (locked until earned), stars, and N1–N6 progress chips.
- An orientation screen with controls and host tips before night 1.
- Endings: beating night 5 shows a newspaper (studio to be demolished, the old watchman missing) and unlocks Night 6. Night 6 shows a creepy pay stub and unlocks Custom Night. A Custom Night at all-20 shows a sign-off card. One star for each.
- Custom night: sliders 0–20 for all five hosts, plus presets.
- P/Esc pauses the game; it also auto-pauses on blur.

## Style
Retro VHS look. VT323 for the UI, a chunky rounded display font for the show logo. Green/amber phosphor HUD: time and night top-right, power and usage bottom-left, key hints above them. Must also work at phone width without overflow.

## Easter eggs
- 6% chance per night that a West Hall poster reads "IT'S STILL ON AIR" with the hosts' eyes crossed out.
- Clicking the booth show poster honks.
- 1/1000 chance on switching to CAM 1 that a sun mascot appears on stage (saved as a ☀ on the menu).
- Typing "sunny" on the menu unlocks everything.

## Quality bar
- Fully playable start to finish with no console errors.
- Night 1 is beatable on the first try with plenty of power left. Night 5 needs skill. Night 6 is hard.
- Comment the code by section: utils/save, textures, puppet models, office, rooms, menu scene, post-processing, audio, game state & AI, input, UI, render loop.

- The axis is the top edge, so each cut face is a semicircle.
- The cut faces are slightly puffy and every seam is rounded.
- It sits on a small flat patch of its round rind.

Regions:
- Flesh: long fluffy red minky.
- Rind: a white band along the outer edge of both faces.
- Skin: green, with dark jagged stripes running pole to pole around the wedge's axis.
- Seeds: short-pile felt teardrops pointing in toward the axis, a few on the front face around the face, more on the back.

Front face: two bead eyes, rosy cheeks, and an embroidered smile thread laid into a short-pile groove.

Limbs: two brown felt legs stuck out in front, and two stubby felt cloth arms at the wedge's ends.

Actions:
- Toddle: walk on the legs.
- Rock: seesaw forward and back on the rind with a synthesized giggle.
- Wave: arm waves and hops with a toy squeak.
- Topple: fall onto its back, then get back up.
- A finger boop on the face makes it giggle and rock; it also rocks now and then when idle.

prompt.text:
Create a high-end cinematic and educational 3D animation in Three.js explaining how a Tesla-style electric motor works.

The animation must have an EXACT FIXED DURATION OF 40 SECONDS.

Do not make the animation shorter or longer than 40 seconds.

Final output:
Exact duration: 40.0 seconds
Resolution: 1920x1080
Aspect ratio: 16:9
Frame rate: 30 FPS
Total frames: 1200
High-quality anti-aliasing
High-resolution textures
Smooth deterministic animation
Extremely realistic visual quality

The overall visual quality should resemble a premium automotive engineering visualization or a high-end technical product commercial.

Build a detailed electric motor assembly inspired by the permanent-magnet AC motors used in modern Tesla vehicles. Do not use Tesla logos or branding.

FIXED TIMELINE

0–5 seconds — Hero introduction
Show the fully assembled electric motor suspended in a dark premium studio environment.

Use:
cinematic lighting
realistic brushed aluminum
copper
steel
magnets
insulation
bearings
realistic reflections
ambient occlusion
realistic shadows
subtle depth of field

Use a slow cinematic orbit around the motor.

During the final part of this section, make the outer housing partially transparent to reveal the internal structure.

5–11 seconds — Internal components
Move the camera closer and reveal the internal motor components.

Clearly show:
stator
copper windings
rotor
permanent magnets
motor shaft
bearings
housing
cooling channels
electrical connections

Highlight the important components one at a time.

Use floating labels with short technical names.

Keep non-highlighted components slightly darker or semi-transparent.

11–19 seconds — Exploded view
Create a dramatic and highly detailed exploded-view animation.

Separate the motor into many individual mechanical components along the motor axis.

Include:
outer housing
front cover
rear cover
bearings
shaft
rotor core
rotor magnets
stator core
copper windings
cooling components
seals
electrical connectors
fasteners

Keep every component perfectly aligned.

The viewer must clearly understand where every piece belongs.

Move the camera slightly through the exploded assembly while highlighting the major components.

Near the end of this section, smoothly begin reassembling the motor.

19–28 seconds — Electromagnetic operation
Finish reassembling the motor.

Explain how electricity creates rotation.

Visualize three-phase AC current flowing through the stator windings.

Use animated electrical pulses inside the copper coils.

Visualize the rotating magnetic field around the stator using elegant semi-transparent magnetic field lines, arrows, or vector effects.

Show how the rotating magnetic field interacts with the permanent magnets inside the rotor.

Clearly visualize magnetic attraction and repulsion.

The rotor should begin rotating slowly and gradually accelerate.

Display these short explanations:

"Three-phase current creates a rotating magnetic field."

"The magnetic field interacts with the rotor."

"This interaction generates torque."

28–34 seconds — Technical close-up and power flow
Show a close-up cross-section of the stator and rotor.

Visualize:
magnetic north and south poles
rotating stator magnetic field
rotor magnetic field
electric current direction
torque direction
rotor rotation direction

Optionally show three small animated sine waves representing phases A, B, and C, separated by 120 degrees.

Then visualize the complete energy conversion process:

Electrical energy
→ stator current
→ rotating magnetic field
→ electromagnetic torque
→ rotor rotation
→ mechanical output through the shaft.
Use clean animated arrows to show the energy flow.
34–38 seconds — High-speed operation
Show the motor operating at high RPM.
The rotor should spin smoothly while the stator remains stationary.
Add subtle motion blur.

Show cooling flow through the housing using translucent fluid paths.

Visualize heat being removed from the stator and copper windings.
38–40 seconds — Final hero shot

Transition back to the fully assembled motor.

Show a slow cinematic rotation.

Briefly use a transparent cutaway so the spinning rotor can still be seen inside.

Finish with the text:

"Electrical energy → Electromagnetic torque → Mechanical rotation"
The animation must end exactly at 40.0 seconds.

VISUAL QUALITY

The animation should be:

photorealistic

cinematic

technically believable

futuristic

premium
educational
clean and uncluttered
Avoid cartoon styling.
Use realistic:
machining details
bolts
screws

copper winding geometry

segmented magnets
bearing geometry
cooling channels
metallic surfaces
manufacturing details
Use physically based materials with:
metallic properties
roughness variation
normal maps
realistic reflections

subtle surface imperfections
CAMERA
Use only smooth cinematic camera movement:
slow orbit shots
macro close-ups
controlled dolly-ins

exploded-view fly-throughs

cross-section shots

internal motor views
Avoid:
shaky camera movement
sudden cuts
excessive zooming
unrealistic camera acceleration

ANIMATION REQUIREMENTS
All transitions must be smooth and deliberate.
The exploded-view sequence should be one of the main visual highlights.
All mechanical components must separate and reassemble with precise motion.
Electrical currents, magnetic fields, torque indicators, and rotor rotation must remain synchronized.

The entire animation must use the same fixed 40-second timeline on every execution so the prompt can be used as a repeatable benchmark between different AI coding and 3D generation systems.

SCENE & LOOK
- Full-screen canvas on a soft watermelon-flesh pink studio background: vertical gradient #ECB3AB → #F7CFC7 (lighter band in the middle) → #E8A9A0, used as the scene background.
- A big oblong watermelon lying on its side along the X axis: half-length 1.38, radius 0.98, blunt barrel-like ends, small dimples at both ends, slightly flattened belly, subtle surface unevenness. Start in a 3/4 view (about -0.32 rad around Y, 0.1 rad tilt), camera FOV 30°, framed to fill ~80% of the height.
- Rind pattern under the fur: light green (#A8D66B) with 16 dark green (#1C4D1C) stripes running stem to blossom, with ragged finger-like edges (sine meander + value noise), plus a pale cream "field spot" on the underside. Each hair takes the colour of its own root, so the stripes stay crisp through the fur.
- A short, dried, ribbed stem stub at one end with a slightly domed pale cut cap, and a thin curly helical tendril springing from beside it.
- One directional light from upper-left-front, wrap diffuse, Kajiya-Kay anisotropic highlight along the hair tangent, darker roots (occlusion by hair height), slight per-hair brightness variation.

FUR (most important: it must look crisp, never blurry)
- Fur length 0.2 units. Hairs grow out along the normal, then bend: combed from the stem end toward the blossom end and draped down the flanks (no whorls at the ends), plus slight gravity.
- Undercoat: shell texturing with ~64 instanced shells of the body mesh that reach only 50% of the fur length. Procedural hair cells in UV space (density scaled so one cell is ~3.4 device pixels at the default view), two hair populations (long + fine underfur), hairs gathering into locks toward their tips, analytic anti-aliased coverage, alpha blending, shells write depth. Fade shells out where the surface is seen edge-on and discard faint fragments, so no dotted rim appears at the outline.
- Guard hairs: ~90,000 individual tapered, camera-facing ribbon strands (instanced, 7 segments each) that follow exactly the same bend function, with a minimum width of ~0.75 px so they stay sharp. Draw them twice: once before the shells and once after (depth-tested), so faint edge fur never hides them and they always lie crisply on top.
- Always render at the device's full pixel ratio (capped at 2) and NEVER lower it for performance. If frames are slow, reduce the shell count first (down to 32), then the guard-hair count.

INTERACTION
- Drag to rotate freely (trackball style) with inertia after a flick. The fur lags behind the rotation through a damped spring and flops back. Gentle idle breeze in the fur; after 3 s without input, a slow auto-turn.
- Mouse wheel / pinch to zoom (smooth dolly). Double-click or "0" resets with an eased animation. Arrow keys rotate.
- Custom cursor: the native grab hand plus a thin dark 46 px ring that follows the pointer and shrinks while dragging. Hovering gently parts the fur under the cursor, as if stroking it.
- Respect prefers-reduced-motion (no idle spin, no breeze).

UI & ROBUSTNESS
- Bottom-left caption: "Fluffy Watermelon" and a hint "Drag to rotate · Scroll to zoom · Double-click to reset" (on touch devices: "Drag to rotate · Pinch to zoom") that fades after the first interaction. Font: Onest from Google Fonts with system fallbacks.
- Guard against a zero-sized container at load: clamp width/height to at least 1 and, every frame, recover from any non-finite camera distance or rotation state.
- Show a small on-page note if the WebGL context is lost or a shader fails to compile, and a fallback message if WebGL is unavailable.

prompt.text:
build a single html file (three.js) that renders a 3x3 puzzle cube in a 1080x1080 square and solves it on camera with a timer.

1. standard colors: white up, yellow down, green front, blue back, red right, orange left. no whole-cube rotations.
2. apply this scramble in wca notation: D2 R' F U2 B' L2 D' R2 U F2 L' B2 U' R D2 F' L U2 B R'
3. solve it your own way - any method, any number of moves. replaying the scramble backwards is not allowed.
4. every move animates in exactly 0.35s with a 0.05s pause.
5. show a timer that stops the moment the cube is solved, plus the current move and a move counter.
6. the cube must actually end fully solved.

<direction>
Dribbble-level UI motion. One shape, no cuts: every state is the same element morphing its size, radius and color while its content swaps with a quick blur.
A cursor controls every change with real clicks and drags. Light warm-gray canvas, black and white components, one clean UI font (Geist).
Springs everywhere, with only a tiny overshoot. The camera zooms so each state fills the entire frame. The last frame matches the first frame, so it loops perfectly.
Banned: bouncy easing, particle bursts, glows, gradients on UI chrome, mismatched icon strokes, dead time, anything that looks like a template.
</direction>

<structure>
120 BPM, 7 bars, something happens on every beat.
Button → loader → check → dynamic island → music player with a play/pause morph → scrub the progress bar → it becomes a volume slider that stretches when dragged past max → a toggle flips on the beat → the knob becomes a liquid tab indicator → the tabs expand into a chart that draws itself, with a tooltip on hover → it collapses into ⌘K → type to filter → enter → toast → back to the button.
</structure>

<build>
One HTML file, square 1440x1440. Every style is calculated from time inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, no timers, no state carried between frames.
Springs use closed-form step responses. A value that changes targets multiple times is the sum of one spring per change, so it remains a pure function of time.
The tab indicator's two edges follow different springs, so the leading edge stretches ahead of the trailing one. Use the same trick for the toggle knob.
Drags use direct manipulation: while the cursor is held, the value is calculated from its position. On release it springs back from wherever it was.
Analyze the song with numpy to find the beat grid and start on a downbeat. Position every UI sound by its measured peak.
Render with Playwright: 4 subframes per frame, blended with ffmpeg tmix for motion blur at 60fps.
Render one frame per beat before the full render. Fix anything off the grid, cramped or difficult to read.
</build>

<gotchas>
Never put will-change on anything the camera scales or the text becomes blurry.
Text that swaps inside a morphing container needs its own enter and exit timing or it overlaps.
Make the final frame identical to the first, including cursor position and speed, or the loop stutters.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me the state list on the beat grid before writing any code.
</start>

prompt.text:
Build a single self-contained HTML file (inline CSS and JS; the only external script is Three.js r128 from https://t.co/0wHkZvIHwv) called "Reef Lagoon": an interactive top-down view of a sunlit Maldives-style lagoon where the user throws sea creatures into the water and watches them swim. Output the complete file, no placeholders, no omitted sections.

CAMERA AND LAYOUT
- Perspective camera straight overhead (height ~26 world units, up vector (0,0,-1)). Fit the vertical FOV so the visible water is about ±8.4 units in the short screen direction; the long direction scales with the aspect ratio. Recompute on resize.
- The whole screen is water. One world unit is roughly 1 m at toy scale: dolphin ~2.4, white shark ~3.3, hammerhead ~3.1, orca ~4.5, humpback ~6, turtle ~1.35 shell length, manta ~1.6 length / 3.2 wingspan.

WATER SIMULATION
- GPU ripple height field (ping-pong float/half-float render targets, about 440 texels on the long side, stepped at 90 Hz). Update: average of 4 neighbours, velocity += (avg − h)*1.8, velocity *= 0.9935, h += velocity, h *= 0.9993. Absorbing "sponge" edges, so waves leaving the screen don't reflect.
- Drops are queued (x, z, radius, amplitude, foam) and applied with a smooth cosine bump; a second channel stores foam that diffuses and fades.

RENDERING (draw order per frame)
1. A tileable animated caustics texture (512², mipmapped).
2. A shadow pass: creature geometry projected along the sun onto the floor, rendered from the main camera into a half-res target with MAX blending.
3. The underwater scene into an off-screen target. Its alpha stores depth*0.22, which later scales refraction and blur.
- Floor: a large heightfield mesh. Depth goes from ~1.35 near the bottom of the screen to ~4.3 at the top, with gentle undulation.
- Coral heads come from noise masks: raised 1–1.4 units, warm ochre/purple/yellow colours with knobbly and brain-coral detail, plus a rubble ring around them.
- Pale sand with soft irregular ripple shading.
- Lighting: ambient + sun × (base + caustics focused by the Laplacian of the ripple field) × shadow × drifting cloud shadows (large slow noise).
- Water absorption along the light path plus the view path, e.g. T = exp(−(0.30, 0.058, 0.04)·path), plus depth-based turquoise→blue scatter.
4. A full-screen water-surface pass. Each pixel is ray-cast through the inverse view-projection to the plane y=0.
- Surface normal from the ripple field + scrolling wind-ripple gradient noise + a gentle swell.
- Refraction: offset sampling of the underwater target, with chromatic split and depth blur.
- Fresnel sky reflection with clouds, sun glints, foam, splash craters (a short-lived analytic bowl around each impact; brighten it, never let it go dark), and an optional whirlpool funnel with spiral foam arms.
- Mild tone curve.
5. An overlay pass, depth-tested, drawn after the surface: creatures above water, water droplets (point sprites, gravity 20), soft mist sprites, rain streaks, expanding ring quads, and a drop-target marker.

CREATURES (procedural geometry, no external models)
- Local frame: nose at +x (x=0.5), tail toward −x, up +y, body length 1.
- Body: lofted elliptical cross-sections along x. Half-width W(u), half-height H(u) and centre offset C(u) are Catmull-Rom curves through control points, where u runs 0 at the nose to 1 at the tail. Flatten the belly, cap the ends, compute normals from the grid.
- Fins: thin double-sided sheets made as bilinear patches between a root chord and a tip chord, with bowed leading and trailing edges.
- Species:
1. Great white shark: slate-grey back with a ragged countershading line to a white belly, gill slits, tall triangular dorsal fin, big swept pectorals with dark tips underneath, crescent tail with a longer upper lobe.
2. Great hammerhead: flat wide cephalofoil with eyes at its tips, bronze-grey colour, tall sickle dorsal fin.
3. Humpback whale: near-black back, mottled white belly with throat pleats, knobs on the head, very long scalloped white pectorals, small dorsal hump, serrated flukes.
4. Orca: black, with the white eye patch, white chin, belly and flank lobe, grey saddle behind a towering dorsal fin, paddle-shaped pectorals.
5. Bottlenose dolphin: beak and melon forehead, dark cape over grey flanks and a pale belly, curved dorsal fin.
6. Green sea turtle: domed shell with scute pattern and amber streaks, pale belly plate, scaly head, long front flippers and small rear flippers.
7. Manta ray: diamond-shaped swept-back wings, curled horn-like fins at the mouth, whip tail, black top with white shoulder chevrons, white spotted belly.
- Draw each species as one InstancedBufferGeometry. Per-instance data: position, orientation quaternion, (swim phase, wave amplitude, turn, fin phase), (scale, alpha, body arch, fin amplitude), (seed, water-class flag, wetness, flipper angle offset).
- Vertex shader:
- Swimming body wave: side to side for sharks, up and down for whales, orca and dolphins, none for turtle and manta.
- Amplitude envelope grows toward the tail, plus turn curvature and arch.
- Rotate each cross-section to stay perpendicular to the bent spine.
- Rotate flippers on hinges about the body axis.
- Manta wing beat travels outward with amplitude ∝ |z|^1.45.
- Sample the GPU water height at the vertex for the waterline.
- Render each species in three passes: under water (discard fragments above the local water height, tint by water), above water (discard below), shadow (project to the floor). Also render card thumbnails with the same materials.
- Fade with an ordered (Bayer) dither. Lighting: sky/ground ambient, sun diffuse with caustics under water, glossy specular that increases when wet, rim light, eyes as dark spheres in the shader.

BEHAVIOUR
- Swimming: wander steering inside the screen (stay above the bottom dock UI), separation between creatures, preferred depth with floor clearance, pitch toward the target depth, roll into turns, currents from the whirlpool.
- Whales, orcas and dolphins periodically surface to breathe and spout: droplet column plus soft mist sprites plus a blow sound. Humpback spout is bushy, orca tall, dolphin a small puff. The humpback dives fluke-up.
- Sharks often cruise with the dorsal fin cutting the surface and leaving a V-wake of small drops.
- Turtles surface to breathe; mantas glide with wing beats.
- Dolphins porpoise-leap often; orca, humpback, shark and manta occasionally breach. A breach means rising fast, launching out of the water with an exit splash, then re-entering in the species style below.
- Tapping the water makes ripples. Sharks, dolphins and orcas come to look at the spot; turtles and mantas flee.

ENTERING THE WATER: EACH SPECIES DIFFERENT (the core feature)
- Tapping a creature card throws the creature from the card's screen position (projected onto the water plane, y=0.6) along a ballistic arc to a random free spot.
- Per-species gravity (whale 6.2, orca 7.5, dolphin 11, others 10) and flight time (whale 1.8 s, orca 1.5, hammerhead 1.3, manta 1.35, shark 1.2, dolphin 1.15, turtle 1.0). Start velocity: vy = (−y0 + ½gT²)/T.
- In the air, orientation is scripted against flight progress τ ∈ [0,1], relative to the trajectory pitch, and blended in from the start orientation over the first 22%:
- Shark: noses steeply down for a knife entry; tail thrashes.
- Hammerhead: corkscrews, two full rolls.
- Humpback: rolls onto its back (≈2.75 rad) and levels out, pectorals raised, body arched: a backflop.
- Orca: rolls onto its side (≈1.5 rad) and levels out.
- Dolphin: follows the arc for a clean head-first dive.
- Turtle: wobbles with flippers flapping into a belly-flop.
- Manta: forward somersault (−2π) into a flat wing slap, wings beating.
- Each entry has its own splash: a crater drop plus several drops along the body line for long animals, expanding rings, a droplet crown with species-specific counts and speeds, mist, bubbles, and sound.
- Dolphin: tiny "rip" splash.
- Sharks: tall crown; hammerhead adds spiral droplets.
- Humpback: huge white curtain (~500 droplets), mist and a low boom.
- Orca: big side splash.
- Turtle: low flat plop.
- Manta: wide low sheet of spray and a sharp slap.
- After entry the creature decelerates under water with a bubble trail, slerps back to its swimming orientation over 1.6–3.2 s (the whale rolls back over from its back), then swims.
- Dragging a card holds the creature above the water under the pointer (with a target ring on the water) and drops it on release with its own entry style.
- The user can grab any creature from the water (pick by distance to its projected body axis), carry it, and throw it back.

UI (English)
- Frosted-glass dock at the bottom: 7 creature cards with thumbnails rendered from the real models and a short description each ("Knifes straight in", "Corkscrew dive", "Backflop breach", "Lands on its side", "Clean arc dive", "Belly plop", "Wing slap"). On phones show short names.
- Tool buttons: Rain (streaks, ring ripples, dimmer sun), Whirlpool (draggable vortex that carries creatures), Calm, Clear (all creatures swim off and fade), Sound (synthesized Web Audio: splashes, plops, blows, slaps, booms, occasional humpback song, dolphin whistles, orca calls, ambient water), Hide UI.
- Top-left name plate "Reef Lagoon" with a live creature count; toasts and a hint line.
- Keyboard: 1–7 throw creatures, R W C M H.

QUALITY AND ROBUSTNESS
- Works on desktop and mobile (touch, pointer events, no horizontal overflow) and in both WebGL2 and WebGL1.
- Adaptive pixel ratio when frames are slow.
- Caps: 24 creatures total, max 3 humpbacks.
- Start with two dolphins, a turtle, a shark and a manta already swimming; a humpback breaches 1 s after load.
- Show a toast for runtime errors and lost WebGL contexts.

prompt.text:
You're a motion director and creative coder. Make a finished music video for [song file], built entirely in code and rendered frame by frame.

Concept: [your idea in one or two sentences]
Look: [palette, mood, references]
On-screen text: [title only / none / lyrics]
Deliver: [full song or mm:ss to mm:ss], [16:9 / 9:16 / both, each recomposed, not cropped], [fps], H.264 + AAC for [platform]

How to work:
1. Analyze the song before any visuals. Split it into bands or stems and export per-frame features plus a timing map (beats, bars, sections, hits). Every visual event reads from the map and is listed in it.
2. Give each musical element one visual job that serves the concept. Keep one idea transforming across the song instead of cycling effects.
3. Storyboard with timings and 3 style frames, get a fresh critic's verdict on them, then a 4-second end-to-end test before the full build.
4. Make every value a pure function of the frame number. Render offline, encode with the original audio (gain only).
5. After each full render, send it to fresh critic subagents that never saw the build, each returning ranked problems with timestamps and a ship / one more pass verdict:
- sound-off: retells the story from a silent 2 fps contact sheet
- sync: every cut, hit and visual event within 1 frame of the timing map
- QA: specs, palette, text, artifacts, measured on the frames
- director: brutal critique against the brief
- one per extra aspect ratio: composition and platform UI zones
6. Fix render bugs first, then the biggest problem; re-render; log each round with before/after numbers. If critics conflict, the brief wins.
7. Stop after [5] rounds or when the bar passes. The final pass checks only for breakage.

The bar: exact duration, size and fps; frame one finished; no still over 0.5 s; cuts and hits within 1 frame; audio unedited except gain, about -14 LUFS, true peak under -1 dB; text readable and inside safe areas; understood with the sound off.

prompt.text:
Build a single self-contained HTML file: an interactive low-poly 3D diorama of a rural Japanese railway station in spring, using Three.js (ES modules from a CDN). No external models or images — generate all geometry from primitives in code and paint textures (grass, signs) on <canvas>.

Style: a floating diorama block (grass top, layered earth and stone sides) on a soft pastel sky gradient. MeshToonMaterial with a 3-step gradient map, dark ink outlines (OutlineEffect), soft directional shadows, bright saturated palette.

Scene:
- A single railway track across the block, running into green tunnel hills with concrete portals at both ends.
- Concrete platform with a yellow tactile strip, a shelter with a corrugated roof, benches, a hanging clock, a small station building with a teal gable roof and a "春風駅" sign, a station name board (はるかぜ / Harukaze, with neighbouring stations), vending machines, bins, lamps, fence.
- A road crossing the track with a level crossing: striped poles, crossbuck, red flashing lamps, barrier arms; road markings and "止まれ".
- Utility poles with sagging wires, overhead catenary, small village houses, a vegetable patch, bushes, and cherry trees with puffy pink blob crowns and fallen petals painted on the grass.

Animation:
- A two-car commuter train (white with a pink stripe, pantograph) comes out of one tunnel, stops at the platform, then departs into the other; clipping planes hide it inside the tunnels. Loop every ~32 s.
- Crossing lamps blink alternately and the arms lower before the train passes, then rise.
- ~460 instanced sakura petals drifting in the wind.
- Slow auto-orbit camera; OrbitControls for drag and zoom.

UI (English): bottom-left title "春風駅 / Harukaze Station" with a small caption; bottom-right glass toolbar with Day / Night, Orbit on/off, and Train (call the next train). Night mode: dark sky with stars, lit windows, lamp point lights with additive glow sprites, glowing crossing lamps and train headlights.

Technical: merge static meshes by material into a few dozen draw calls; use a seeded random so the scene is identical on every load; responsive down to phone width; respect prefers-reduced-motion.

prompt.text:
Build a single self-contained HTML file (Three.js via CDN, no other assets) that is the 2026 version of the "ball bouncing inside a spinning hexagon" test.

Scene: a large hollow hexagonal prism (a 3D hexagon) slowly spinning on two axes at once. Inside it, a smaller hexagonal prism spins the opposite way, and inside that, a tiny one. Three nested spinning cages. The cage walls are see-through panels drawn only as clean outlines with a very light flat tint, so every ball inside stays clearly visible.

Physics (write your own, no physics library):
- Start with 1 ball inside the innermost cage. Every 2 seconds a new ball spawns, up to 300, each with its own random size, mass and color.
- Real gravity, friction, restitution and spin. Balls must collide with each other and with the rotating walls, picking up the wall's velocity at the contact point so they get flung realistically. No tunneling through walls, no jitter when balls rest on each other.
- When a ball hits a wall hard enough, that wall panel cracks and eventually breaks into flat shards that also obey physics, so balls can escape into the next cage outward.
- The outer cage never breaks. Escaped balls pile up at the bottom of it.

Look, clean cel-shaded style:
- Toon shading on everything: 2 or 3 hard shading bands per object, crisp dark outlines (inverted-hull or edge detection), flat colors from a small tasteful palette.
- A plain flat light background (soft off-white or pale gray), with a simple flat floor shadow under the cage.
- No bloom, no glow, no neon, no lens flares, no motion blur, no particle haze, no gradients, no transparency stacking. No visual artifacts: no z-fighting, no flickering outlines, no shadow acne, no aliasing (use antialiasing and a sensible pixel ratio).
- Impacts get small, flat cartoon "pop" marks that vanish quickly, not sparks.
- It should look like a clean animated illustration, not a tech demo.

Camera: a slow, smooth orbit by default, plus drag to orbit and scroll to zoom.

Sound: synthesize everything with the Web Audio API. Each collision makes a soft pitched tone based on ball size and impact speed, so it turns into gentle generative music as it gets chaotic. Breaking panels get their own sound. Keep it quiet and pleasant, never clipping.

UI: a small, minimal flat panel in the corner (no glassmorphism) with sliders for gravity, spin speed, bounciness and ball count, a "slow motion" toggle, a "reset" button, and an FPS counter. It must stay at 60fps with 300 balls on a laptop.

prompt.text:
Build an interactive 3D web page: a live "bench study" of the **Lamborghini FL3**, the air-cooled three-cylinder diesel that powered the Lamborghini 2R tractor (1961 to 1967), from the years before Lamborghini built cars. Visitors should be able to start the engine, rev it, load it, cut it open, watch the cooling air, and take it apart. The page should feel like a beautifully printed technical plate that happens to be alive.

## Hard rules

- **Everything procedural.** No 3D models, no Blender, no textures, no image files, no audio files. Geometry, materials, drawings and sound are all generated in code.
- **three.js (WebGL)**, vendored locally, ES modules with an importmap, no build step. It must run from a plain static server.
- **60 fps** on a recent laptop at 1440x900 and on a retina display.
- **Desktop:** the whole sheet fits a 1440x900 viewport with no scrolling.
- **Phone width:** the sheet becomes a vertical scroll with nothing cut off. On touch, horizontal drags turn the engine and vertical swipes scroll the page.
- **No em dashes** anywhere in the copy.

## The engine: facts

Only these figures are published. Use them exactly:

- 3 cylinders, inline, air-cooled, direct-injection diesel, Lamborghini type FL3
- bore 92 mm, stroke 110 mm, 2,193 cc
- 39 hp (29.1 kW) at 2,200 rpm
- electric starter, Bosch injection
- about 2,000 2Rs sold between 1961 and 1967
- factory colours: orange and light blue ("celeste")

The external layout, from photographs of a restored 1962 2R:

- the engine block painted celeste
- an axial cooling blower in a round housing at the front, belt-driven from the crank, with a wire guard
- a sheet-metal air cowl along the cold side
- individual finned cylinder barrels and finned heads, held down by long studs
- a silver inline injection pump on the hot side, with three copper high-pressure lines up to the injectors
- twin fuel filters
- a black vertical exhaust stack with a silencer and a flapper rain cap
- an oil-bath air cleaner
- a dynamo, a starter motor, and a flywheel with a ring gear

Everything else is an assumption and must be labelled **modelled** on the page:

- compression ratio (about 17:1), rod length, valve timing
- idle (about 700 rpm) and high idle (about 2,350 rpm)
- torque curve, friction, airflow, temperatures, fuel use

Never dimension an assumed size in the drawings.

## Art direction: a 1960s Italian two-ink print

It must not look like a Victorian parchment plate or a generic blueprint. Think of a page from an Italian factory manual or a mid-century industrial catalogue, printed in the tractor's own two inks.

- **Paper:** ivory offset stock (about #EEE9DC) with fine paper grain and soft, uneven ink absorption.
- **Inks:** arancio (#E0561C), celeste (#58AED6 for the print, a deeper #3F9DD0 for the painted engine) and near-black (#1C1B19).
- **Type:**
- Bodoni Moda for display: a huge "FL3" with the 3 in arancio, and an italic "Lamborghini" above it.
- Archivo for labels (wide, letter-spaced small caps).
- IBM Plex Mono for numbers.
- Every label carries its Italian term in small italic Bodoni (for example: Hand throttle *acceleratore*).
- **Print details:**
- registration marks in the four corners and a colour bar in the margin
- a thin double frame and a running head across the top: "Bench study · *banco prova*", "Air-cooled diesel · three cylinders · direct injection", "Sheet 03"
- a giant celeste numeral "3" printed faintly behind the engine, slightly out of register
- **Layout at 1440x900:**
- left column: title, deck, lede and the controls
- centre: the 3D engine
- right column: four live instruments
- bottom strip: four live drawings and a readings card

Copy:
- Kicker: "Lamborghini Trattori · 1961–1967"
- Deck: "Three cylinders. No radiator."
- Lede: "Before the supercars, Lamborghini built tractors. The 2R of 1961 carried this engine: 2,193 cc of direct-injection diesel and no radiator, cooled by a belt-driven blower and cast fins. About 2,000 were sold by 1967, and tractor money paid for the move into cars in 1963."

## The 3D model

Build the FL3 to its real proportions: 92 mm bore, 110 mm stroke, cylinders about 150 mm apart, crank axis as the origin.

Exterior parts:

- crankcase with main-bearing ribs and mounting feet, oil sump, timing case, flywheel plate
- three separate finned barrels, with the fins flattened where neighbours meet
- three finned heads with rocker covers and long studs
- blower with a spinning rotor, stator vanes and a guard
- V-belt around the crank, dynamo and blower pulleys
- air cowl with a stencilled "FL3 · raffreddato ad aria"
- intake runners into the oil-bath air cleaner with a glass pre-cleaner bowl
- exhaust manifold, silencer and a flapper cap that lifts on each exhaust pulse at idle
- injection pump with a governor housing whose throttle lever follows the hand throttle
- copper injector lines and a leak-off line, injectors, twin fuel filters
- starter motor whose pinion slides into the ring gear while cranking
- a small name plate reading "MOTORE DIESEL · FL3 · CV 39 · 2200 g/min" (no company logo anywhere)

Moving internals:

- crankshaft with counterweights, pins 120 degrees apart, turning clockwise seen from the blower end
- connecting rods, pistons with rings and a combustion bowl
- camshaft at half speed with lobes timed to the valve events
- tappets, pushrods, rockers, valves and springs that compress, all driven by the same valve-lift curves the simulation uses

Materials and setting:

- **Materials:** glossy celeste enamel with subtle procedural grain, rougher on castings than on sheet metal. Steel, alloy, copper and heat-darkened exhaust.
- **Stand:** the engine sits on an **arancio test stand**.
- **Lighting and floor:** a soft cast shadow and a contact shadow lands on the paper itself (a transparent canvas over the page).
- **Life at rest:** the engine rocks slightly on its mounts against the gas torque.

## The simulation

Write it as a pure, testable module.

- **Kinematics:**
- exact slider-crank piston motion and rod angle
- four-stroke cycle over 720 degrees, firing order 1-2-3, one firing every 240 degrees
- **In-cylinder pressure:**
- polytropic compression and expansion with a double-Wiebe heat release (fast premixed burn plus a slower diffusion burn), tabulated by fuel level
- calibrate the heat release so that full fuel at 2,200 rpm gives exactly 29.1 kW at the flywheel
- peak pressure lands around 70 to 75 bar at full load
- **Crank dynamics:**
- integrate with sub-steps of about 2 degrees of crank, so the instantaneous gas torque gives real speed ripple at idle and real compression pulses while cranking
- flywheel inertia about 0.8 kg·m²
- **Governor and load:**
- an all-speed mechanical governor with about 120 rpm of droop and a little fuel-rack lag
- the hand throttle sets the governed speed between idle and high idle
- the PTO brake applies a load that rises with the square of speed, so 100% load at 2,200 rpm needs exactly full fuel
- **Starting:**
- the starter cranks at about 250 rpm
- the charge needs a few compressions before it lights, the first cycles misfire and burn rich, and that black smoke leaves the stack
- the engine catches in about 1 second and the starter disengages
- **Stopping:**
- friction rises with speed, plus blower drag rising with the square of speed
- an unfired cylinder gives back less than it took to compress (heat lost to the fins), so the engine stops about 2 seconds after the fuel is cut at idle
- **Temperatures:**
- head temperatures come from about a quarter of the fuel's heat going into the metal, removed by blower air that rises with engine speed
- full load settles around 160 to 175 °C
- run thermal time 30 times faster than real time and say so

The simulation emits events with timestamps: crank, fire, misfire, exhaust valve opening, caught, stop, stalled. Events raised between steps (the key) must not be lost.

## Interaction

- **Ignition key:** a round bakelite-and-steel switch. Click (or Space) to start and stop. It shows Start, Cranking or Stop.
- **Two levers:** the hand throttle shows the governed rpm, and the PTO brake shows a percentage. Style them as notched quadrants with orange lever knobs.
- **Four views** (keys 1 to 4), each with a smooth scripted camera move:
- **Painted.**
- **Cutaway:**
- a section plane through the cylinder axes, with cut faces printed as a light arancio hatch
- parts lying wholly in the removed half (pump, filters, exhaust, starter, pushrods, cam) disappear
- pistons, rods and crank stay whole
- a combustion glow fills each chamber as it fires
- **Airflow:**
- everything except the barrels and heads fades to a paper-grey ghost
- barrels and heads show a temperature ramp from deep celeste to arancio
- particles are drawn in through the blower guard, run along the cowl, cross the fins and leave warm on the pump side
- particles are drawn through the metal like the flow arrows of a technical illustration
- **Exploded:**
- waits until the engine has stopped, then separates the parts along sensible axes and holds the crank still
- each part gets a callout: English name in small caps, Italian term in italic, and a leader line to an orange dot
- labels sit on a paper backing and never overlap
- **Other controls:**
- Slow motion (S) eases time to 1/25
- a Sound toggle
- Reset view
- drag to orbit, scroll to zoom
- **Narration line:** a single italic line in the console that reacts to what is happening. Examples:
- "Key turned. The starter pinion meshes with the flywheel and spins the engine at about 250 rpm."
- "Squeezed about 17 to 1, the air gets hot enough to light the diesel. No spark plugs."
- "It caught."
- "Idling near 700 rpm: three power strokes every two turns, one every 240 degrees."
- "The hand throttle sets the governor, which opens the rack until the engine holds that speed."
- "Full PTO load at 2,200 rpm: the rack is wide open and the FL3 makes its rated 39 hp."
- "No water anywhere. The blower pushes air down the cowl, across the fins, and out warm on the pump side."
- "Fuel cut. It runs down and rocks back on its last compression."
- Each view also gets a line of its own.

## Live instruments (Canvas 2D, ink on paper)

1. **Tachometer:** a period Italian dial, 0 to 25 x100 rpm, with an arancio arc above rated speed and an hour meter whose tenths drum rolls.
2. **The cycle:** a 720-degree wheel with three rings (one per cylinder, offset 240 degrees). Power is arancio, exhaust grey, intake celeste, compression hatched. A pointer follows the crank and a dot flashes at each firing.
3. **Indicator diagram:** the live P-V loop for cylinder 1, with the full-load loop dashed for reference, a dot at the current state and the peak pressure labelled.
4. **Chart recorder:** scrolling chart paper with an rpm pen in black and a power pen in arancio.

Below the drawings, a **readings card**:

- live values: speed, power, torque, fuel (l/h), cooling air (m³/min) and head temperature
- marked "live, modelled"
- a footnote listing what is published and stating that the page is an independent study, not affiliated with Lamborghini

Power and torque are measured at the flywheel, so they never overshoot the rated 39 hp during transients.

## Live drawings: blueline prints of the running engine

Front, Right side, Plan and **Section A-A** are real orthographic renders of the same running model, not illustrations. Ink them in a shader like 1960s diazo prints:

- render normals and depth, then draw blue outlines from silhouette, crease and depth edges
- shade with a celeste 45-degree screentone
- print an arancio hatch wherever the section plane cuts metal
- the diazo paper and its faint grid are printed by the shader itself
- add centre lines and numbered cylinders
- Section A-A cuts through cylinder 1 so you see the piston moving. It dimensions only the published bore (Ø 92) and stroke (110), with TDC and BDC lines marked PMS and PMI.

## Sound (Web Audio, synthesised)

- **Exhaust:** each pop is scheduled from the simulation's own exhaust-valve events at the correct sub-frame time. It is not a looped sample.
- **Layers:**
- diesel knock at each injection
- blower roar and a blade-pass tone tracking speed
- valve-gear whirr
- a starter whine that strains on each compression
- a solenoid clunk on start and stop
- the flapper cap ticking at idle
- a soft metallic cue when the engine comes apart and a seating clunk when it goes back together
- **Slow motion** spaces the pops out and deepens them.
- **Mix:** run everything through a compressor. It must never clip.
- **Autoplay:** audio starts on the first user gesture.

## Deliverables

- the page: `index.html`, `css/`, `js/`, with three.js vendored in `vendor/`
- a tiny no-cache static server (`https://t.co/H56Y9tkCZm`)
- a README that separates published facts from modelled ones
- a headless Node check of the simulation that asserts:
- 29.1 kW at 2,200 rpm
- peak pressure 60 to 85 bar
- catches within 3 s
- idles between 650 and 750 rpm
- full load holds about 2,200 rpm and 39 hp
- heads pass 120 °C under load
- it stops after the fuel is cut
- optional: a frame-exact video capture script (virtual time at 60 fps, a drawn cursor with click rings, the sound rendered offline from the simulation's event log so it stays in sync)

## Done means

1. The sheet loads with no console errors and holds 60 fps.
2. Turning the key cranks, catches with a dark puff and settles near 700 rpm.
3. Full throttle plus full PTO load reads about 2,200 rpm and 39 hp, and the P-V loop peaks around 73 bar.
4. Every view works, including Section A-A cutting through the moving piston.
5. The exploded view waits for the engine to stop, and its labels are all readable.
6. Every figure that is not published is labelled as modelled.
7. At 1440x900 nothing overflows, and at phone width nothing is cut off.

prompt.text:
Build a single-file WebGPU page "Peach Jelly" in the style of a "Material Studies" specimen sheet (light studio backdrop #E2DFDA, italic serif title, a specimen control panel on the right, live readouts bottom-left, collapsible "Inside the experiment" notes; responsive with a stacked phone layout and a no-WebGPU fallback card).

Subject: half a peach made of translucent jelly, cut along its suture, lying skin-down with the cut face up and its stone seated in the hollow.

Geometry: a signed distance field for the fruit — a sphere slightly longer from stem to blossom end, with a stem dimple, a faint point at the blossom tip and the suture crease along one side of the rim, belly gently flattened on the floor — cut at the equator, minus an almond-shaped hollow for the stone (flattened, broad faces parallel to the cut, blunt toward the stem). Simulation mesh: a snapped hex lattice, 5 tets per cell (~700 particles / ~2500 tets), node layers exactly on the floor and the cut face, nodes forced out of the stone. Render surface by surface nets, embedded in the tets by barycentric weights, with one normal-smoothing pass per frame so reflections don't pick out tet kinks. The stone gets its own high-resolution mesh: deep wormy furrows (mostly lengthwise) and little pits carved by displacement, a low keel round its edge, a small point at the blossom end; groove depth rides in the vertex material id for shading.

Physics (CPU, XPBD, 60 Hz, 10 substeps): per-tet co-rotational shape matching + volume constraints, stiffer skin, edge-relative damping, floor friction, pointer grab with twist. The stone is a rigid body (position, quaternion, ellipsoid inertia) with frictional contact against every particle and sampled floor contacts. Nodes lining the hollow are held by soft adhesion bonds that peel (floor of the hollow first, lip last) under a sustained net pull measured in the half's best-fit rigid frame — never from brief knocks; a loose stone resting in the hollow is drawn home and re-bonded with a soft grace period. Grabbing the stone moves it as a whole and it can be thrown. Buttons: nudge, reset, "Pop the stone" / "Put the stone back", pause, ¼ speed, show mesh; sliders for firmness and damping; readouts mass, volume %, grip %.

Rendering (WGSL): shadow map + top-down contact-AO map, scene pass (floor, stone, bubbles) with linear depth in alpha, back-face thickness pass, refracting jelly with Beer–Lambert absorption and scattering. Regions from rest-space SDFs: golden flesh; a ruby ring hugging the stone, broken up irregularly, with fine red fibres streaking out; the skin's blush bleeding a little way into the flesh. Skin: yellow with patchy red blush and pale flecks, a velvet sheen at grazing angles (nectarine: smooth and glossy). Stone: woody reddish-brown, dark furrows with shreds of red fibre, soft key shadows, low sheen. Varieties: Yellow, White, Nectarine. UI text in English.

prompt.text:
【段落 1：开工 ＋ 平面图】
我想用 three.js 做一座黄昏时刻的寺庙，最后输出成 70 秒的视频。
规则：不准用任何 3D 模型、贴图或照片，所有东西全用代码生成。
先不要渲染画面，先输出一份场景平面图 ⁠layout.js⁠：定义好主殿、五重塔、拱桥、莲花池、山门的位置和尺寸，单位用“米”。之后所有的代码都只能从这个文件里读取坐标。
太阳定在西南偏西方向、地平线上方约 7 度，打暖色光。
【段落 2：分身施工】
平面图确定后，开启 6 个 Sub-agent（子智能体）并行施工，每个 Agent 负责一个区域：地形、池塘（莲花、锦鲤）、主殿、五重塔、拱桥、树木。
每个 Agent 只能修改自己的文件。
全局材质（朱漆、金箔、青铜、屋瓦、木头）统一写在 ⁠materials.js⁠ 里供大家调用。
随机数一律使用固定种子（固定 Seed），保证每次打开渲染出来的样子一模一样。
（注：这一步记得附上几张高清的寺庙照片，给 AI 作为参考）
【段落 3：镜头调度】
安排 10 个镜头，每个镜头 7 秒。
每个镜头都从一个小物件的特写开始（灯笼、莲花、风铃、佛像面部等），再慢慢拉远露出整个场景。镜头开头先在特写停留片刻，中间加速拉远，结尾放慢缓动。
最后一个镜头，从逆光的枫叶拉远，最后过渡到整座寺庙的全景俯拍（航拍视角）。

prompt.text:
Recreate the environment in these 10 reference images in 3D, using only code. No assets, no textures. It's a big environment: a lake with mountains and forest around it.

The task has two parts:
1. Build the 3D environment.
2. Make a cinematic one minute video that showcases the world, and render it.

The environment:
- Make it look 99.9% like the reference images. Don't stop early because you think it's good enough. Iterate until you reach 99.9% similarity. It might take days, I know. There's a lot to do.
- Colors: 100% clean, the best colors. Compare your colors with the colors in the images. Most of the time the colors come out wrong and a bit too grey, and coloring is one of the most important things. Light and shadows have to match too.
- Water: get the water right. The colors, the physics, everything should look perfect.
- Trees: they can't look fake. Give them much better textures and make the forest denser.
- Mountains: better textures and a better vibe.
- Rocks and terrain: good rock textures and a lot more detail in the small stones and the terrain.
- Distance: render everything. Don't render the trees only half of the distance. Trees far away need detail too, also in the half-wide shots.
- In the end it should look like a real place to the human eye.

The video:
- Cinematic, like a drone-filmed movie. That's only a comparison: no drone UI, no drone noises, just a clean video.
- Start with a really good scene and show the best stuff first. Then slowly show more and more: for example, you're behind a rock and can only see a bit, then the camera flies up and you see a really nice view.
- Every six or seven seconds, switch to a different place. Sometimes fast, sometimes slow.
- Sound: calm nature sounds and epic background music. The music has to be really good.
- Output: high resolution and ultra-wide, so you can see the trees on the other side as well. Clean and not buggy. Keep full quality, even if it takes longer.

How to work:
- I don't have a strong GPU, so keep that in mind. You can use my GPU, on CPU it would take a lot of time.
- Work in rounds and send me screenshots after each round, without pausing. If it still needs improvement to reach 99%, start the next round right away.
- Don't start the final video before everything is really good. Send me the screenshots first, wait for my approval, and only then render.
- Don't stop until it's really done and really good.

If you have questions, ask me now. Otherwise, build as long as you can and make it awesome. Go and cook.

prompt.text:
Turn the attached image into a seamless looping GIF (~15s, 15fps)
styled as a surveillance-camera "subject analysis" sequence:

1. ACQUIRE – desaturated CCTV feed with REC, camera ID, running
timecode; a search reticle locks onto the subject.
2. SILHOUETTE – background dims to a dark grid; AI detection boxes
(head, torso, limbs + confidence scores) pop in; a scan line
turns the subject into a flat silhouette.
3. STRUCTURE – silhouette becomes a glowing wireframe (edges +
triangle mesh), then a pose skeleton with joint angles.
4. FEATURES – real colors return; an "ENHANCE" zoom on the face;
animated callouts with typed labels for 4–5 key features.
5. PALETTE – extract the 6 dominant colors (k-means); swatches fly
from the image into a panel with hex codes and percentages.
6. IDENTIFY – "TARGET LOCKED" + ID card (class, threat level,
match %), then a glitch back to frame 1 for a seamless loop.

Keep the original artwork intact (segment it, don't redraw it).
Minimal HUD: white + one accent color, monospace font, a stage
progress panel in the emptiest area of the frame, no text over
the face. Export GIF + MP4.

prompt.text:
Build "Geyser Jelly" — a single-file interactive WebGPU diorama for a "Material Studies" series: a volcanic Icelandic island set inside a translucent block of jelly sea, viewed as a tabletop object on a pale paper studio backdrop.

TECH
- One self-contained HTML file: plain JS + WGSL, no libraries, no network requests (Google Fonts optional). WebGPU only, with a clean fallback screen if WebGPU/adapter is missing or the device is lost.
- Block 5.2 × 5.2 units, sea level at y = 1.0. The block can be tipped by dragging its ground/sides; it springs back and quivers like jelly (shear + squash wobble applied to everything inside in the vertex shader).
- Sea = linear shallow-water sim on a ~168² grid (heights + face velocities, a little surface tension, damping), fed by the block's tilt. Render the water with refraction of the scene behind, colored absorption through the jelly, light shafts, caustics on the bed, foam/white water, a bright meniscus on the cut faces. Cut faces of the ground show candy-coloured strata, basalt, tephra bands and turf.
- Sun shadow map, MSAA, HDR with a soft shoulder tone map. Fixed-step simulation (240 Hz bodies, 120 Hz water). Expose a debug handle on window for tests.

THE ISLAND (procedural height field + ground cover: moss, grass, sinter, scoria)
- Back-left: a scoria cone volcano with a real crater bowl holding a lava lake (dark crust plates with glowing seams), patchy summit snow. A lava channel runs from a flank vent with a spatter cone down into the sea, glowing ribbon with drifting crust; it keeps glowing under the jelly water; constant steam where it meets the sea. Warm lava light on nearby ground.
- Back-right: a grassy plateau that ends in sheer columnar-basalt cliffs on its seaward side, three basalt sea stacks with grassy tops, puffins on the ledges, a small square orange lighthouse.
- Middle: a geothermal valley — a pale sinter mound with orange bacterial runoff streaks, the geyser pool (blue over a dark vent), two milky-turquoise hot springs and one clear deep-blue one, a grey bubbling mud pot with expanding rings, fumarole steam. A timber boardwalk arcs round the front of the geyser with tourists on it, with paths to the jetty, the church and the lagoon.
- Front-left: a milky blue lagoon in white silica banks, a timber deck with a ladder, a black-timber bathhouse with a turf roof, bathers drifting up to their shoulders.
- Front-right: a meadow with three turf houses (grass roofs; white, red and tarred gables), a little white church with a red roof and spire inside a turf wall, a flagpole with a fluttering Icelandic flag, a fenced paddock with five Icelandic horses (chestnut with flaxen mane, black, grey, palomino, bay).
- A jetty on piles out to a T-head where a whale-watching boat berths; a small ticket hut. Black-sand beaches, lava boulders, kelp, urchins and sea stars on the sea floor.

THE GEYSER (Strokkur)
Cycle every ~15–20 s on its own: refill → rest (simmering, occasional bulges) → surge (three growing heaves, gurgling, wisps of steam) → a turquoise dome swells and quivers → it bursts: a white churning water column (20–35 m in the UI; 1 unit = 20 m) shoots up ballistically, hundreds of streaked drops rain back down and drift with the wind, the column breaks apart from the bottom up, a big steam cloud rolls off downwind, the sinter goes dark and wet, then the pool drains with a gurgle. Tourists raise their arms and cheer; some hold up phones during the surge.

THE VOLCANO
Tremor: the block shakes, ash billows from the crater, lava bombs fly (thud and smoke on land, hiss, steam and a splash at sea, glowing then cooling), the lava lake rises and brightens, the flow speeds up, horses bolt round the paddock, puffins take off, and the geyser goes off.

LIFE
- Humpback whale (knobbly head, long white flippers, grooved pale throat, broad flukes): cruises offshore, surfaces and blows 2–3 times (spray plumes), arches and shows its flukes as it dives, stays deep, avoids the boat and shallow water. About once a minute (or on demand) it breaches: sounds deep, turns to an open spot, rushes up, leaps clear while twisting, crashes onto its back with a huge splash, foam and a ring wave across the bay that rocks the boat.
- The boat "Hafdís" (old oak fishing boat: dark blue hull, red bottom, white wheelhouse, passengers in bright jackets): lies at the jetty ~40 s, then casts off and does a loop round the bay on a smooth filleted route, slowing right down when the whale is near, rides the waves with heave/pitch/roll, makes a wake, puffs exhaust, comes back alongside.
- Atlantic puffins: stand on the cliff edge and stacks, stretch their wings, whirr out over the bay, land on the water, dive and chase fish underwater, fly home and land.
- People: 9 tourists on the boardwalk (sometimes shuffle to another spot), walkers on the paths and jetty, 6 bathers in the lagoon. Horses graze, wander, trot when startled. A school of fish in the bay flees threats.
- Steam, ash and spray are soft translucent puffs drawn after the water with premultiplied alpha, broken up with noise, rising, spreading and drifting downwind.

UI
- Left: eyebrow "MATERIAL STUDIES", big italic serif title "Geyser / Jelly.", subtitle "A volcanic island with a geyser, set in a block of jelly sea." Bottom-left: "How to play" with the line "Set off the geyser. Shake the volcano. Watch for the whale." and a small paragraph of hints. Top-right: status pill "WebGPU · Live".
- Right glass panel: buttons Erupt / Tremor / Breach / Cast off (→ Full ahead); disabled with labels like "Surging…", "Erupting…", "Draining…", "Refilling…" when not ready. A thin liveliness meter. Tallies: Eruptions, Tallest (m), Breaches. Status lines "Strokkur: Resting 5 s / Surging / Erupting · 24 m / Draining / Refilling 68%" and "Hafdís: Alongside 18 s / Casting off / Under way 40% / Whale ahead / Coming alongside".
- Flavours: Blue lagoon (milky aqua), Lingonberry (red), Licorice (smoky dark). Sliders: Firmness, Wave damping, Wind. Buttons: Reset, Pause, Sound on/off, View.
- Interaction: tap the geyser, the volcano, the whale or the boat to trigger them (hand cursor on hover); Space sounds the boat's horn and puts the puffins up; drag across the water to make waves; drag the ground or the block's side to tip it; drag empty space or right-drag to orbit; wheel/pinch to zoom. On phones the panel becomes a bottom sheet with a "Controls" bar; no page scroll at any size.
- Sound: synthesized with Web Audio, only for events — surge bubbling, dome thump, eruption roar and spray hiss, drain gurgle, tremor rumble with rattles, bomb thuds and hisses, whale blow, breach rush and splash, boat horn, puffin and mud plops. No background ambience.

QUALITY BAR
Charming, legible miniature scale; nothing sticks through the water surface by mistake; no NaNs under stress (repeated tremors, eruptions, breaches, shaking, stirring). Verify with headless screenshots and an end-to-end browser test of every control, the geyser cycle order, the boat round trip, the breach, taps, flavours, sliders, pause, camera, mobile sheet and fallbacks — with zero console errors.

prompt.text: Build "Harbor Jelly" — a single self-contained HTML file (no external requests, no libraries) that renders an interactive 3D diorama with WebGPU/WGSL: a small working container harbor set inside a square block of wobbly, translucent jelly sea, sitting on a paper studio backdrop. It belongs to a series called "Material Studies", so match that look: warm paper background, serif italic display title ("Harbor Jelly."), small uppercase eyebrow "MATERIAL STUDIES", a status pill top-right ("WebGPU · Live"), a frosted control panel on the right, and a "How to play" line bottom-left. English UI. Light theme only, by design. THE BLOCK - A 5.2 × 5.2 block seen from a 3/4 orbit camera. The ground and sea are cut flat at the block's sides, so you see candy-coloured soil strata in cross-section, and the sea's cut faces show everything underwater through the jelly. - The water is a real-time linear shallow-water simulation on a staggered grid (heights at cell centres, velocities on faces) with a little surface tension, so it feels like jelly. Render it with refraction, absorption by depth, caustics projected onto the floor, light shafts, a Fresnel studio reflection, foam (wakes, splashes, a shoreline lace) and a bright meniscus on the cut edges. - The whole block can be tipped by dragging its side. The water sloshes to the low side, the jelly shears and quivers, then it settles flat again. THE HARBOR (layout) - Along the back runs a vertical concrete quay wall, with rubber fenders, bollards, ladders, and mussels and weed crusting it below the waterline. - Left part: a container terminal. A flat asphalt yard with painted lines, concrete strips with two crane rails, light towers, and a small terminal office. Hundreds of colourful containers are stacked in neat rows. Each is a ribbed steel box with door ends and darker corner posts, drawn as GPU instances in about ten liveries. - Right part: an old stone fishing quay with a cobbled promenade, a corrugated fish-market shed and lamp posts. A timber pier stands on mussel-covered piles with cross-bracing, with two small fishing boats moored alongside. - Behind it all, a town climbs a grassy hill: three rows of gabled houses in Nordic harbour colours (falu red, ochre, white, pale blue, mint, pink) with tiled or slate roofs, white-framed windows, doors and chimneys. There is a white church with a green copper spire, and some round trees. - A rubble breakwater shelters the fishing harbour, with a concrete crown wall. Big rocks sit near the crest, smaller weedy ones tumble down under water. On its head stands a red-and-white banded lighthouse with a gallery and a glass lantern, whose lamp slowly turns. - In the open basin: two small yachts swinging on their moorings (white hulls, coloured stripe, fin keels visible through the jelly, furled sails), yellow mooring buoys, and a green channel buoy, all bobbing on the waves. - On the floor: pale sand with drifts of silt, weed tufts, stones, starfish, an old anchor with chain, a lost tyre. THE SHIP'S DAY (fully automatic loop, about 100 s) 1. A small feeder container ship (navy topsides, red antifouling, white accommodation block at the stern with bridge wings, funnel with a yellow band, turning radar, visible propeller) lies alongside with containers on deck, 6 bays × 4 rows × 2 tiers. 2. Two ship-to-shore gantry cranes on the rails, one red and one blue, each with portal legs, a backreach with a machinery house, an A-frame with forestays, a hinged boom, a trolley with a hanging cab, and a yellow spreader on four wire falls. They lower their booms and swap boxes: unload from the tops of the ship's stacks into yard stacks, then load other boxes aboard. Every move is a smooth sequence: travel, trolley out, lower onto the box (tracking the ship's bobbing), latch, hoist, trolley across, lower, unlatch. Cranes never get closer than their leg width; an idle crane moves out of the other's way. 3. When the work is done the trolleys park, the booms swing up, and a tug comes round to the bow. The tug has a black hull, white and red superstructure, a tyre fender all round, a big bow fender, and puffs of funnel smoke. It passes a tow line and backs away, pulling the bow off the quay while the ship swings out. Then the line is cast off, the tug pivots on the spot and goes home, and the ship sounds her horn. 4. The ship sails a lap of the harbour along a smooth path, past the lighthouse. She rides the water on several sample points (heave, pitch, roll) and hands the displaced water back to the sim, so she leaves a real bow wave, wake and white water. 5. Meanwhile the tug goes out to a standby spot. When the ship stops off the quay, the tug noses in and pushes her sideways onto the fenders, with prop wash churning. Then it backs off, the booms come down, and the cranes start again. - Keep everything collision-free (ship and tug vs. quay, breakwater, pier, yachts and buoy; no grounding). Check it with a headless node test. LIFE - Fish schools (mackerel, herring, small orange wrasse) as boids that stay in the water and under the hulls, scatter from fingers, splashes and moving ships, and come to food. - Moon jellyfish: glassy pulsing bells with four pink rings, frilly oral arms and a fringe of tentacles. They drift with the water flow. - Herring gulls (white body, grey mantle, black wingtips, yellow bill with a red spot). They circle, bank and glide, and land on perches: lamps, roof ridges, the church spire, the lighthouse gallery, the crane apexes, the ship's mast, the tug, the yachts' masthead. Perches on moving things move with them. They all take off when the horn sounds, and some dive at food. - Steam puffs from the ship's funnel on the horn; tiny bubbles caught in the jelly. CONTROLS (right panel; bottom sheet on phones) - "Cast off" sends the ship early (cranes finish the box in hand). At sea the button becomes "Call her in" and hurries her home; it greys out while busy. - "Horn" (also Space) plays a synthesized WebAudio ship horn: two low detuned sawtooth reeds a fifth apart, low-passed, starting only after a user gesture. It also blows steam and scatters the gulls. - "Feed the fish" scatters pellets off the end of the pier; fish rush in and gulls swoop down. - Tally: Boxes moved / Voyages / Fed. A ship status line ("Unloading 3 / 8", "Loading", "Booms up", "Tug coming", "Casting off", "At sea 40%", "Coming in", "Berthing"). A small activity meter. - Flavour swatches change the water colour and strata: Sea glass (teal-mint), Blueberry (deep blue), Lime. - Sliders: Firmness, Wave damping, Tide (±10 cm; the sea level, ships and floating things follow). - Buttons: Reset, Pause, Sound on/off, Reset view. POINTER INTERACTION - Drag across the water to make waves (with a crosshair cursor). - Drag the side of the block to tip it. - Pick up an orange-and-white lifebuoy and throw it. Lifebuoys float flat on the waves, bounce off the pier, buildings and breakwater, and are shoved aside by the ship and tug. - Drag empty space or right-drag to orbit; scroll or pinch to zoom. - On phones: touch orbit, pinch zoom, and a collapsible bottom sheet for the controls. RENDERING DETAILS - Pipeline: shadow map → caustics pass → opaque scene (with a distance buffer) → back-face pass of the water → water pass over a copy of the scene → tone map + dither. - Moving rigs are static vertex buffers whose vertices carry an object id; about 24 object transforms (position + quaternion) live in the uniform buffer. Cables are drawn with one end in each object's frame, so they stretch: crane falls, forestays, the tow line. - Material kinds in the prop shader: matte paint, glass, gloss steel, roof tiles, timber grain, corrugated sheet (normal-perturbed ribs), dressed-stone masonry, rubber, rock, glowing lamps, swaying weed, and hulls with antifouling below a boot-top line. - The jelly shear and squash wobble applies to everything inside the block. QUALITY BAR - Smooth on a laptop; simulation under about 2 ms per frame. - A friendly fallback screen if WebGPU is missing or the adapter fails. - No console errors, no page scroll. Respect prefers-reduced-motion. - Ship it with a headless test of the choreography and a Playwright end-to-end test.

prompt.text:
Build a real-time WebGPU soft-body "jelly" study of a watermelon wedge that you can cut with a steel knife, in an editorial "Material Studies" page style (serif title "Melon Jelly.", muted paper backdrop, side panel, English UI, mobile-friendly). Geometry: a thick triangular watermelon wedge with a rounded green rind, a pale white layer, and translucent red flesh with dark seeds and a few air bubbles. Sim: CPU XPBD on a tetrahedral mesh, fixed 60 Hz step with 10 substeps. Each tet uses a co-rotational shape-matching constraint with finite compliance, which also flips inverted elements back out, plus a near-incompressible volume constraint so a stretched slice necks in. The rind is about 3× stiffer than the flesh. Damping acts only on relative velocity along edges. Floor contact uses Coulomb friction. Grabbing is a soft, reach-limited attachment to a patch of particles, and scroll or a second finger twists it.

Two tools, Hand and Knife:
- Knife: the user draws a stroke across the slice. Read on the surface, that stroke defines a vertical blade plane. Every piece is stored as a rounded convex outline in the slice's rest plane. For each piece the plane crosses, fit the piece's current pose with a best rotation, carry the plane back to rest space as a straight line, and split the outline along it.
- The cut: prebuild both halves as fresh tet meshes on release. An animated steel knife lines up over the stroke, comes down, and first presses a groove into the jelly. When it breaks through, swap in the new pieces, which inherit the position and velocity of the flesh they came from, and the blade wedges the faces apart on its way to the board. Draw the blade behind the jelly surface so the buried part is seen refracted.
- Pieces: every piece is its own soft body that can be grabbed, stretched and cut again, and pieces collide with each other instead of passing through.

Render: a smooth surface mesh plus the seeds and bubbles, each vertex embedded in a tet by barycentric weights so they ride the wobble. WGSL passes:
- floor, seeds and bubbles first;
- back faces, to get the thickness each view ray crosses;
- front faces with refraction by that thickness, Beer–Lambert absorption, milky scattering in the pale layer, a back-lit glow at thin edges, Fresnel reflections of a procedural studio, and GGX highlights;
- a soft key shadow on the floor tinted by the jelly, plus contact AO from a top-down height map.

Varieties: Crimson, Golden, Rosé. Controls: Hand/Knife tool toggle, firmness and internal damping sliders, "Give it a nudge", Reset, Pause, ¼ speed, Show mesh, plus mass/volume/kinetic readouts and an "Inside the experiment" notes drawer explaining the physics, cutting and rendering.
