prompt.text:
Create a visually impressive interactive 3D cutaway jet engine experience in Three.js.
The result should feel like a premium technical visualization or futuristic engineering showcase.
The first few seconds must have a strong wow effect and immediately hook the viewer.
Core idea:
Build a detailed jet engine in 3D with a clean outer shell, and let the viewer explore the inside through cutaway, x-ray, and exploded-style views.
Main requirements:
Build a full 3D jet engine from scratch in code
No pre-made 3D models
Use Three.js
Prefer a single HTML file unless a few small extra files are truly necessary
The project must run locally in the browser
The engine should include:
front fan blades
compressor stages
combustion chamber
turbine stages
exhaust section
outer shell / nacelle
internal shaft structure
visible airflow path
Interactions / modes:
assembled mode
cutaway mode
x-ray mode
exploded view mode
airflow visualization on/off
throttle or power slider
auto-rotate camera option
orbit controls
Animation ideas:
engine startup sequence
fan spins up first
inner stages accelerate
combustion chamber ignites
hot glowing section appears in the core
exhaust flow becomes visible
subtle vibration / mechanical life
Visual quality:
polished lighting
premium materials
good contrast between outer shell and internals
smooth transitions between modes
readable labels or callouts for key engine parts
cinematic presentation
strong sense of depth
The first seconds should feel especially strong:
for example, begin with a clean hero shot of the engine, then smoothly reveal the cutaway and ignite the core.
Make it feel detailed, technical, and visually satisfying rather than toy-like.

prompt.text:
Build a single-file HTML + Three.js interactive scene called "Jelly / Eyeball."

Look: premium product render on a clean white background. One large gummy eyeball sits on the floor in the center - milky translucent jelly sclera with fine red veins, a glowing blue iris with radial fibers, a glossy black pupil and a clear wet cornea bulge on top. A red gummy optic nerve trails behind it on the floor. Soft colored glow and a soft shadow underneath. Around the edges: small jelly pumpkins (purple, green, orange), jelly beans and candy corn, all glossy and translucent. Physically based materials (transmission, clearcoat), environment reflections, ACES tone mapping, soft shadows.

The eye is a real soft body - deformation happens in the vertex shader so the sclera, iris, pupil and cornea all bend together:
1. It always watches the cursor, and keeps finding you even after it rolls.
2. Tap it - a gooey dent with a ripple, jelly eyelids blink, the pupil contracts, and it does a small hop.
3. Grab and drag it - the grabbed spot stretches toward the cursor like taffy into a teardrop. Lift it up and it dangles and sways with gravity.
4. Flick and release - it gets thrown with the hand's velocity plus a slingshot recoil from the stretch. It squashes and stretches along its velocity in flight, splats on the floor and walls with a big squash, bounces, rolls (the iris rolls with it), then wobbles and rights itself to look back at you.
5. Pull it sideways and let go - it snaps back like a slingshot.
6. Grab the nerve - it is a verlet rope, so you can lift the eye by it and swing it around.
7. Double-tap - hypnotized: the pupil dilates and the gaze spins in circles.
8. Hard landings make it dizzy - its eyes wander for a moment.

Jelly secondary motion everywhere: volume-preserving squash on impacts, shear wobble when it accelerates, ripples from pokes.

UI: elegant serif italic title "Jelly /" with "Eyeball." in the iris color top-left, small kicker "Nº 12 / Soft goods · October", short grey subtitle. Small white control panel top-right: iris color swatches (changes the iris and title color), sliders for Pupil and Wobble, a live "Mood" status (Curious / Startled / Stretched / Airborne / Dizzy / Dangling / Hypnotized), a "Blink" button and a "Pour candy" button that rains gummies that bounce off the eye and dent it. Bottom hints: "Drag to stretch · Flick to throw · Tap to poke · Pull the nerve". Price "2.90 €" bottom-right.

Smooth 60fps.

prompt.text:
Build a single-page web toy called "Yard Box": a real-time 3D scene rendered as pixel art, showing a courtyard football box behind a four-storey panel apartment block on a floating island. Use three.js r160 (ES module via import map from jsDelivr, plus BufferGeometryUtils). English UI. Original design only — no real brands, places or logos.

RENDERING PIPELINE (the core look)
- Orthographic camera at an isometric angle (elevation ≈31°, azimuth π/4, rotatable in 90° steps with smooth easing; drag sideways or buttons to turn; wheel/pinch zoom 0.7–2.6).
- Render into a small WebGLRenderTarget (half-float, nearest filtering, depth texture) — about 480×300 art pixels at pixel size 3 — no anti-aliasing. Fit the island + the top of the block into the screen area left free by the UI, and snap the camera so the world origin lands on a whole art pixel (static things never shimmer).
- Post-pass ShaderMaterial: texelFetch whole-pixel upscale; depth-based outlines (a pixel > ~0.5 m in front of a neighbour darkens ×0.5); quantize every pixel to the nearest of a fixed ~60-colour palette in OKLab (lightness weighted ×1.35); optional 4×4 Bayer dither (off by default); empty depth = page background colour.
- "Raw 3D" toggle shows the full-resolution MSAA render without steps above. Controls: pixel size slider 2–6, palette / dither / outlines checkboxes.
- Palette: warm concrete greys, cool greys for snow in shade/moonlight, snow and sky blues, turf greens, autumn olives, yellows/oranges/rusts, team reds and blues, skin and wood tones, lamp/window yellows, dusk violets, mint for the boards.

LIGHT AND TIME
- Directional sun/moon with hard BasicShadowMap (2048), hemisphere fill, point lights for two streetlamps (decay 2) and weak doorway lamps. Presets Day / Dusk / Night blended over 1.6 s. Glow materials lerp between on/off colours.
- The block's facade uses an emissive map drawn on a canvas; at night windows glow warm or cool, and random flats switch lights on and off.

WORLD (all boxes, cylinders, extrusions; textures drawn texel by texel on canvases)
- Rounded floating slab: grass top over soil over rock.
- Football box: rounded-rectangle boards (22×12 m, mint green, plank lines, a gate with an open door), netting on posts above the boards at both ends, mini goals (3 m × 2 m) with alpha-tested nets, turf texture with mowing stripes, worn goalmouths/centre and white markings.
- Panel block along one long side: 4 floors, facade drawn panel by panel with windows and curtains, two entrances with canopies, random balconies, roof details; an asphalt strip with two benches and hedges.
- Dollhouse cut: when the camera looks from the block's side, hide the floors, roof, balconies and canopies and show a section of the ground floor instead — low cut walls with a dark cap, rooms with coloured floors, rugs, sofas, tables, wardrobes, TVs (glowing at night), pot plants, stairwells with steps and post boxes; room floors glow warm at night.
- Playground (swing that actually swings, slide, sandbox), birches with white trunks and dark marks, painted-tyre flower beds, a parked car, a washing line with swaying sheets, two lamp posts.

PEOPLE AND DOG
- Kids as rigs of ~17 boxes (bigger heads), posed every frame with two-bone IK: running stride, kicks keyed as back-swing → strike → follow-through, keeper stance, sideways dives, catch/hold/throw, goal celebrations (airplane arms).
- Three grandmothers sitting on the benches (cheer on goals), a small kid on the swing.
- A box-built dog that lives by the benches.

GAME LOGIC
- 3v3: two field players + one keeper per team (RED attacks +x, BLUE −x), first to 5, then a new game; scoreboard with score, game number, status line and games won.
- Kick-off from the centre; open play with dribbling by small touches, passes leading the receiver, shots aimed inside a post at random height with angular error growing with distance and pressure, tackles; players get behind the ball before kicking (feed-forward on a rolling ball), squeeze in at an angle when the ball is against the boards, avoid goal frames; a scramble poke if nobody can reach a still ball for 3.5 s.
- Keepers hold position, come out for slow loose balls, read shots after a 0.1–0.3 s reaction delay with some error, dive, catch or parry.
- Ball physics in 4 substeps: gravity, ground bounce (lower in winter), boards (lively below rail height, dead in the netting above), posts and crossbar, the goal net, legs in the way. Status flashes: GOAL!, SAVED!, WHAT A SAVE!, OFF THE POST!, OFF THE BOARDS, TACKLE.
- Every 100–170 s (or on a button) the dog runs in through the gate, grabs the ball, runs loops away from the kids for ~5 s, drops it and trots home; it gives up if the game resets.

SEASONS (Summer / Autumn / Winter)
- Summer: poplar fluff drifting. Autumn: yellow/orange canopies, leaves falling from the birches, leaf litter on the ground, olive grass. Winter: snow on the ground, roofs, benches, car and boards; bare trees; falling snow and kicked-up snow spray; kids wear hats; the ball turns orange.

INPUT AND UI
- Click the player on the ball to shoot, his teammate to pass, the pitch to make him dribble there; keys S, P, D, Space, Q/E or arrows.
- Layout: title and caption top-left, lit pixel-font scoreboard top-centre, a narrow control rail on the right (Time, Season, Game, View), a hint bottom-left, a fold-out "How it's drawn" panel bottom-right. Fonts: Silkscreen, Rubik, JetBrains Mono. Light and dark themes via CSS tokens; on phones everything stacks under the scene. WebGL2 fallback card.

prompt.text:
Build "Corner Court" — a single-file, real-time three.js (r160, ES module via import map from jsDelivr) page: an isometric diorama of an original street basketball half court on a floating city block, rendered as crisp pixel art. UI text in English.

RENDER PIPELINE
- Orthographic camera at ~31° elevation, azimuth 45° + 90° steps (animated; drag sideways or buttons), wheel/pinch zoom; fit the whole slab into the free screen area.
- Render into a small target (screen / pixel size) with no anti-aliasing; snap the camera to whole pixels.
- Post pass:
- depth outlines (darken a pixel >0.55 m in front of a neighbour);
- nearest colour of a fixed ~54-colour city palette in OKLab (concrete/asphalt greys, sky and night blues, court teal, terracotta/orange, reds, yellows, leaf greens, skin/wood, dusk purples, neon pink); optional 4×4 Bayer dither;
- whole-pixel upscale via texelFetch; the background (depth = 1) is the page colour.
- Hard shadows (BasicShadowMap); flat-shaded Lambert low-poly.
- Puddle reflections: render the scene mirrored about the ground (scene.scale.y = -1, ground meshes and rain hidden) into a second target, sampled at gl_FragCoord in the ground shader.
- "Raw 3D" mode: the same scene at full resolution with MSAA.

SCENE
- A ragged-edged slab: grass over soil over rock.
- An asphalt pad painted texel-by-texel at 10 px/m: teal inside the 6 m arc (straight corner lines), terracotta key, white lines, free-throw and restricted circles, cracks, worn paint, a stencilled "COURT 7".
- Hoop: padded navy pole, arm, backboard with its square, orange torus rim, and a line-segment net that sways when the ball goes through.
- Chain-link fence behind the hoop (alpha-tested diamond texture).
- A brick corner shop with an awning, lit windows, a pink "OPEN" neon sign and a vending machine.
- A long wall with an original sunset-city mural.
- A sidewalk with a bench and two seated spectators.
- Floodlights, a streetlight, low-poly trees, hedges, a dumpster, a fountain, a bike rack with two bikes, a hydrant.
- Pigeons that peck and fly off when players or the ball come near.

PLAYERS — procedural rigs of ~17 boxes
- Two-bone IK for legs (running stride, defensive slide, tucked jumps) and arms: dribble hand following the ball, jump-shot set point with release and gooseneck follow-through, layup reach, two-hand dunk, chest pass, rebound/contest reach, celebration.
- Spectators sit, cheer on makes and open umbrellas in the rain.

GAME — streetball 2v2 half court
- Make it take it; 1s inside the arc, 2s beyond; first to 11; win counter.
- Check ball at the top (pass to the defender and back). A change of possession must be cleared beyond the arc.
- Offence AI: dribble to spots, drive when the lane is open, pull-up jumpers when open, layups/dunks at the rim, passes when pressured; the off-ball player spots up or cuts. Man-to-man defence with stance, gap control, steals and contested jumps (blocks).
- Ball physics with substeps: bounces on asphalt, sphere vs torus rim and backboard box, net drag, pole, fences, wall, slab edge.
- Jumpers aimed on a ballistic arc (~50°) with speed/aim noise growing with distance and contest.
- Layups lofted to a peak above the rim so they drop in.
- Rebounds with jumps; out of bounds goes to the other team.
- Score, possession and status messages ("SWISH", "BLOCKED!", "TAKE IT BACK", …) on a lit scoreboard.
- Clicks: the ball handler shoots, his teammate gets a pass, the court sends the handler there. Shoot/Pass buttons.

WEATHER AND TIME
- Day / Dusk / Night lighting presets blended over ~1.6 s; floodlights, streetlight, neon and windows at night.
- Dry / Drizzle / Downpour: rain as short line streaks with splashes. A wetness value rises and slowly dries: the asphalt darkens, puddles spread from low spots in a precomputed depth map and mirror the scene, rain rings flicker in them; feet and the ball splash.

UI
- Pixel display font (Silkscreen) and a clean body font; light/dark themes via tokens.
- Controls: Time, Weather (with a court wetness bar), Shoot, Pass, New game, Pause, Turn left/right, Pixel art/Raw 3D, Pixel size, Palette/Dither/Outlines.
- A "How it's drawn" panel; a stacked mobile layout with no horizontal scroll.

prompt.text:
Build "Offshore Jelly" — a single-file interactive WebGPU diorama in the "Material Studies" series: a stretch of North Sea cut out as a cube of translucent jelly, sitting on a studio floor. Everything is procedural (no external assets, no network), one HTML file with inline JS/WGSL.

THE BLOCK
- A wobbly jelly cube you can grab by its sides and tip; it springs back. Sliders: firmness, damping, wind (0–20 m/s).
- Inside: a shallow-water simulation for the sea surface (waves, wakes, foam, whitecaps), seabed with sand ripples, scour rocks, kelp, boulders, starfish, crabs, urchins, a pipeline, cables and a small wreck. Caustics on the seabed. Dragging the water stirs up waves.
- Waves come from the wind: several wave trains whose height grows with wind speed.

THE SCENE
- A production platform on a four-legged steel jacket (braces, risers, conductors, boat landing, marine growth below the waterline): main and cellar decks, process module, derrick, living quarters, lifeboats, a pedestal crane with a laydown area, a flare boom with a flickering flame and smoke.
- An octagonal helideck with an H, a net, perimeter lights and a windsock.
- Five offshore wind turbines on monopiles: transition piece with yellow platform, boat landing ladder, davit, tower, nacelle, three-blade rotors with red tips, blinking red aviation lights. Rotor speed and power output (MW) follow the wind.
- A rocky skerry with a lighthouse whose beam turns; seals haul out on it.

WHAT HAPPENS
- Supply run: a platform supply vessel comes in from standby, holds station next to the jacket on dynamic positioning (thruster foam), and the crane does four lifts — containers swing on the hook, are set down on the platform and back-loaded onto the boat's deck. Then she sails back to standby.
- Helicopter: flies in from the west, turns into the wind, lands on the helideck; a deck officer walks out; passengers get off. A second press sends it away (spin-up, lift, outbound). Rotor and tail rotor spin, downwash flattens the water.
- Crew boat: a small catamaran sails out to a turbine, pushes its bow onto the boat landing, and technicians climb the ladder onto the platform. Next time she picks them up and brings them home.
- Storm: the wind builds to a gale, waves get big with whitecaps and spray, rain falls, the room darkens, lightning strikes blades, the lighthouse, the derrick or the sea with a flash and thunder. Above cut-out the turbines feather their blades and stop (0 MW); the helicopter is grounded. Then it eases and the turbines restart.

LIFE
- Schools of fish around the jacket and wrecks, gulls that perch on railings and take off on the horn, gannets that plunge-dive for fish, a pod of porpoises, seals, moon jellyfish, crew walking the decks.

CONTROLS & UI
- Buttons: Supply run, Helicopter (take-off when landed), Crew boat, Storm. Space = ship's horn. Tapping a turbine switches it on/off, tapping the supply boat or helideck calls them. Orbit by drag, zoom by wheel/pinch.
- Tallies: Power (MW), Lifts, Flights; status lines for the supply boat, helicopter and crew boat.
- Flavours (jelly colour palettes): North Sea, Curaçao, Blackcurrant.
- Sounds are synthesised with WebAudio and only play for events (horn, winch, set-down, bump, rotor, thunder, rain) — no constant background ambience. Sound toggle and pause.
- Mobile: a bottom sheet with the controls, touch orbit and pinch zoom. Clean fallback message when WebGPU is unavailable.
- Copy in English: "Offshore Jelly. A wind farm and a platform working a stretch of North Sea, set in a block of jelly." — "Call in the supply boat. Fly the crew out. Brew up a storm."

prompt.text:
Apply a dark neon glitch-art effect to the attached video (Python + ffmpeg, frame by frame):

1. Cut out the subject with rembg (isnet-anime for anime/illustration, isnet-general-use for real footage). Make the background pure black.
2. Posterize the subject to 5 brightness levels and recolor it with a 3-color palette on black:
main color for cool/neutral areas (cyan #14b8f0), mid color (violet #6438c4), accent for warm/red areas (magenta #ff2ad4).
Keep it dark: most of the image black or navy, only the highlights glow. Let the color-patch edges crawl slightly with noise.
3. Add a magenta rim light on the subject's left edge.
4. Datamosh: wherever the current frame is empty, keep the previous frame shifted a few px down and faded (melting ghost trails). Also copy ~3% of 24px blocks from the previous frame with a small random offset.
5. Vertical drips: in ~30% of the columns, smear bright pixels upward (up to ~300px) and downward (~150px). Mix 2–8px wide drips with thin vertical scratch lines in the palette colors, denser near the subject.
6. Light grain + vignette. Keep the original resolution and fps, export as H.264 MP4.

Generate an original vaporwave-glitch soundtrack (~-12 LUFS) / make it a seamless loop where the last 1s drips into the first 1s column by column.

prompt.text:
Build a single-file HTML + three.js (r160) scene called "Chalk Square": four square played with a football in a back yard on a floating island. It is a real 3D scene rendered as crisp pixel art.

Rendering: an orthographic isometric camera (drag to turn in 90° steps, scroll or pinch to zoom). Render into a small low-res target with a depth texture, then upscale with texelFetch to whole screen pixels. Add depth-based outlines and quantize every pixel to a fixed ~60-colour palette in OKLab, with an optional Bayer dither. Toggle "Pixel art / Raw 3D", with a pixel-size slider and Palette / Dither / Outlines checkboxes.

Yard: patched, cracked asphalt with a kerb, grass and dirt around the island edge. Around the asphalt:
- a row of lock-up garages with painted, numbered doors and a flat roof that overhangs them;
- a brick transformer booth with a warning sign;
- a poplar with a bench and a grandmother on it;
- a chin-up bar, a carpet rack with a rug, bushes;
- a lamp on a pole and a lamp over a garage door.
Pigeons walk and peck, and flap up onto the roofs when the ball or a kid comes near. A cat on the garage roof follows the ball with its head.

Chalk: a data texture over the asphalt. It holds the 4.8 m square split into four zones (King, Queen, Jack, Dunce) with letters and a crown, plus hopscotch and doodles. Each texel stores its order along its stroke, so the lines can be redrawn progressively.

Game (8 kids, each with a skill, power and style: power / trick / safe / lob):
- Four kids play, four wait in a queue. The King serves by dropping the ball and kicking it after the bounce.
- The ball must bounce once in your zone, then you kick it into another zone. With the two-touch rule you may first cushion it up.
- You are out for: a ball that lands out, lands in your own zone, bounces a second time, or (if set) lands on a middle line. Otherwise a ball on the line is replayed.
- The kid who is out goes to the back of the queue. Everyone below moves up a zone, and the next kid in line enters at Dunce. A kid fetches the ball and throws it to the King.

Ball and AI: real ball physics (gravity, bounces, rolling, softer bounces in puddles, the walls). Each receiver simulates the ball forward, picks the moment it is at foot height, runs to stand behind it and kicks. Shots are a drive, a lob, or a dink just over the line, aimed away from the target kid; everyone picks on the King. Aim and power errors grow with a fast ball, a stretched contact and lower skill, and occasionally a kick is shanked.

Kids: box-rigged with two-bone IK. Poses: run, ready crouch, a kick that strikes at the ball's height, cushion, hold, throw, clap, argue a call, and a crouched walk while drawing chalk.

Time and weather: Day / Dusk / Night (the lamps light the court), Dry / Rain.
- Rain: streaks, splashes, darker asphalt, puddles that mirror the yard via a mirrored render pass, and the chalk washing out.
- The kids shelter under the garage roof. When the asphalt dries, two of them redraw the square and play resumes.

UI (English, light and dark themes, mobile layout):
- A lit scoreboard with rallies, clock + status, the King's current reign, and the best reign.
- A side rail with: Time & weather (with asphalt and chalk bars); the ladder (King / Queen / Jack / Dunce plus "Next up"); Rules (One/Two touches; Liners: Replay/Out); a feed of calls with "Gang up on the King" and Pause; View.
- Click a kid in the square and everyone aims at them. Original design, no real brands.

prompt.text:
Turn the attached footage into a beat-synced, manga-style music edit and send me the finished MP4.

INPUTS (fill in or leave blank; if blank, choose sensibly and tell me what you chose)
- Source footage: [attached]
- Music: [attached track / use the source audio]
- Aspect ratio: [default 4:3 1440x1080; 9:16 1080x1920 for vertical], 24 fps
- On-screen text / credit: [optional]
- Palette: [default: paper #f8f2ea, ink #141012, main accent red #d0141e (shadow #7c0a12), highlight yellow #ffd60a (shadow #f29a00)]

GOAL
The edit should feel like a living manga page: ink lines, screentone, flat accent colours, bold graphic backgrounds, and hard cuts locked to the music. It must look designed, not like a filter over video.

1. STUDY THE MATERIAL
- Go through the footage frame by frame using contact sheets. Catalogue every usable moment: framing, pose, motion peaks, internal cuts, and strong details (eyes, hands, silhouettes, close-ups, crash zooms).
- Analyse the music: BPM, beat grid, downbeats, phrases, sections, energy curve, accents, fills, ending.

2. LOCK THE LOOK (applies to every shot)
- Mask the subject on every frame (rembg isnet-anime for anime or illustration, a human-segmentation model for live action). Check mask quality before relying on it.
- Ink lines via XDoG/DoG, with thickness scaled to the framing.
- Paper base. Mid-tones become halftone dots: fixed screen angle, area-correct radius. The deepest shadows become solid ink.
- Strict palette: paper + ink + one main accent + one highlight.
- Map the subject's most distinctive colour to the flat main accent.
- Map glowing or brightest elements to the highlight.
- Everything else stays monochrome.
- Tune tones per shot so faces read clean (mostly paper, light screentone).
- Give subject cut-outs a thin ink outline when composited over graphics.

3. DESIGN YOUR OWN SHOT VOCABULARY
Based on what this footage does well and what this music needs, define 6-10 recurring shot types. Each type pairs a kind of source framing with a graphic treatment. Draw from this palette or invent your own:
- extreme close-up of a detail with impact shake
- silhouette over a bold graphic (concentric rings, rays, burst)
- clean black-and-white manga panel with a lightened background
- subject cut-out over a graphic ground (halftone texture, printed-page texture, blobs, speed lines, flat colour)
- typographic panel (large vertical CJK or bold type, plus small secondary lines; all text original)
- impact marks (!!, stars, sparkles)
- black or flash frames
- glitch frames (channel split, slice offset, magenta/yellow)
- tinted frames (pink, red, mono)
- halftone-dissolve transitions
- punch-ins and crash zooms
Rules:
- Every type must use something the footage genuinely does well.
- Save the strongest images for the strongest musical moments.
- Briefly justify each type.

4. PLAN A FRAME-ACCURATE EDL BEFORE RENDERING
List start/end frame, shot type, source frames, framing, motion, transition and text for every shot. Rhythm rules:
- Cut 1-2 frames before the beat.
- Mix durations: 3-6 frame hits against 1-2 beat holds, with at least one breathing moment per phrase.
- Build a recognisable 8-beat (or phrase-length) pattern and repeat it, using different source footage each time.
- Let the energy follow the music:
- a calm intro (for example desaturated, with only the highlight in colour)
- dense peaks
- an outro where colour drains, glitches escalate, and the edit fades with the music
- Land gestures and motion peaks in the footage on musical accents.

5. MOTION AND FINISH
- Animate the subject on twos. Keep camera moves (zoom, drift, rotation) smooth on every frame.
- Use shake and scale bumps on hits, with subtle film grain.
- An optional small HUD element (for example a timecode box) is fine.

6. PREVIEW, FIX, RENDER, VERIFY
- Before the full render, render one frame per shot as a preview sheet. Fix composition, mask errors, text cut-offs and palette breaks.
- Render, then review the whole output on contact sheets, fix problems and re-render the affected frames.
- Encode H.264 at CRF ~20-22 with AAC 192k, synced to the music at the same length.

QUALITY BAR
- Every frame could pass as a printed panel.
- No muddy greys, no unmasked background smears, and no accidentally cropped text.
- Dot size stays consistent.
- Outside glitch frames, no more than two colours appear besides paper and ink.

DELIVER
The MP4, plus a short summary of the shot types you invented and where they land in the edit.

prompt.text:
Build a cinematic 3D animation of a white Tesla Roadster performing a rocket-assisted stunt inside a massive nighttime test facility.

Start with a wide shot revealing a towering curved ramp supported by exposed steel scaffolding. Add red illuminated track edges, road markings, and industrial floodlights.

Follow the Roadster as it accelerates up the ramp, climbs vertically, and launches into open air.

At the highest point, switch to a dramatic low-angle close-up. Fire the downward-facing thrusters. Show bright exhaust and thick, rolling smoke that expands naturally beneath the car.

Bring it down onto the track, let the suspension compress on landing, then pull the camera back as it drives forward through the clearing smoke.

Keep the white bodywork readable throughout. Control headlight bloom. Make the wheels rotate correctly and keep the vehicle’s shape consistent between shots.

Add subtle circular HUD gauges for altitude and G-force.

16 seconds. Vertical 9:16 framing. Smooth camera movement.

Make it look expensive. The launch and thruster
